stem: A client using a home blood glucose meter obtains a reading that is much higher than expected shortly after handling fruit. The client has no symptoms of hyperglycemia. Which action should the nurse recommend first?

options.A: Wash and dry the hands thoroughly, repeat the test using the meter and test-strip instructions, and seek further evaluation if the repeat result remains discordant with the clinical picture.
options.B: Immediately increase the insulin dose based on the single unexpected reading without repeating the test.
options.C: Ignore all unusually high meter readings when the client has no symptoms because asymptomatic results are unreliable.
options.D: Rinse the fingers with water but leave them wet before retesting because moisture improves capillary blood sampling.

rationale: A is correct. FDA guidance states that blood glucose meter accuracy depends partly on how the test is performed and specifically instructs users to wash and dry their hands and closely follow the meter instructions. ADA 2026 further states that a meter result that is discordant with the clinical picture should be retested and, if concern persists, confirmed by laboratory testing as appropriate. Residue on the fingers can contaminate a capillary sample, so repeating the test after proper hand preparation is safer than changing therapy from one unexpected value. B risks a medication error. C dismisses potentially important hyperglycemia. D is incorrect because hands should be dried before testing.
educational_objective: When a home glucose-meter result is unexpected or clinically discordant, verify testing technique by washing and drying the hands and repeating the measurement before acting on a potentially erroneous value.
source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration; American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
source_document_title: Blood Glucose Monitoring Devices; Diabetes Technology: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_version_date: Current FDA device guidance accessed 2026-08-17; ADA Standards of Care 2026 published December 8, 2025
source_locator: FDA ‘Blood Glucose Monitoring Devices’ — safe use and accuracy depend on test performance; wash and dry hands before testing and follow meter instructions. ADA 2026 Section 7, ‘Glucose Meter Inaccuracy’ — a reading discordant with the clinical picture should be retested and may require laboratory confirmation
source_claim_supported: Correct capillary glucose testing requires clean, dry hands and adherence to device instructions; an unexpected result should be repeated before treatment decisions are made, with further confirmation if discordance persists.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential; validate unexpected diagnostic/monitoring results and reduce risk from acting on inaccurate data
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — verifying an unexpected home blood glucose meter result
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source checklist-style technique item into a clinically consequential verification scenario. The final version uses current FDA guidance on washing/drying hands and following meter instructions plus ADA 2026 guidance to repeat discordant readings, and reclassifies the item from Basic Care and Comfort to Reduction of Risk Potential.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.clinical_category: blood glucose monitoring / meter accuracy / result verification
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified directly against current FDA blood-glucose-monitor guidance and ADA Standards of Care 2026 Section 7. Both support proper technique and repeat testing when a reading does not fit the clinical picture.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A uses only supported actions and avoids prescribing a universal laboratory-confirmation threshold. The fruit-handling context makes contamination plausible without asserting that contamination definitely caused the reading.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; it verifies technique and repeats the measurement before treatment is changed.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; acting on one possibly contaminated result can cause inappropriate insulin dosing and hypoglycemia.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; lack of symptoms does not justify ignoring a potentially important result.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; FDA advises washing and drying hands before testing.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A addresses both possible preanalytic error and the need to reassess a discordant result safely.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are immediate responses to the same unexpected meter value.
audit_findings.blueprint: Reduction of Risk Potential is appropriate because the nurse is preventing harm from an inaccurate monitoring result.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked hand-contamination plausibility, FDA wash/dry instruction, discordant-result retesting, medication-change risk, lab-confirmation wording, category mapping, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
